chunks: "External EMI is anything from outside the board: transmitters like cell phones, Wi-Fi and broadcast, nearby motors and switching supplies, mains noise, ESD, and surges.
It gets in the same way the board radiates, through antennas.
Any loop of traces picks up magnetic field, any long trace or cable picks up electric field, and cables bring in common-mode currents and conducted noise on power and signal lines.
What it does depends on the circuit.
A field of 10 volts per metre at 100 megahertz induces about 21 millivolts in a 10 square centimetre loop, which is bigger than a 20 millivolt sensor signal.

Even if the RF is far above the circuit's bandwidth, semiconductor junctions rectify it: an op-amp input stage or ESD diode demodulates amplitude-modulated RF into a DC offset or audio-frequency buzz, so a sensor reading shifts when a phone is nearby.
Digital circuits can see glitches on resets, interrupts and clocks. ESD and surges can reset or damage the board.
So I'd treat the inputs and connectors as the entry points: keep loops small, filter and protect at the connector, use differential signalling, and keep high-impedance nodes short."
